reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: a held computed slot over one entity, refreshed by its OIMComputedCollection at the read after the frame
reading.floor: set a dirty flag on write, recompute on read if dirty
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR IS A REAL MEMO AND DOES THE SAME JOB: it is invalidated by the write, it recomputes once however many writes landed, and it answers the same number. ONE HALF OF THIS CAVEAT WAS TRUE OF THE OLD ENGINE AND IS NOT TRUE OF THIS ONE. It said the floor recomputes LAZILY at the read where ours recomputes EAGERLY during the frame, so a value nobody reads was free for the floor and paid for by us. A derivation is a slot that nothing ever marks now — it is asked, not woken — so both sides are lazy and a value nobody reads is free on both. WHAT THAT LEAVES IN THE RATIO is the settle itself: ours compares the clock stamp of every source against the stamp it last derived at and only then runs the body, where the floor reads one boolean. WHAT OURS STILL BUYS AND THE FLOOR CANNOT: the graph. A memo over another memo has to be invalidated by hand and in the right order; `oimRefreshComputedSlot` refreshes its source computeds first. The 1024 derivations are the slots of ONE `OIMComputedCollection` keyed by position, each held, so the read is `getValueForSlot` on an identity resolved before the clock and no key is looked up. That is not exercised by the one-level derivation here, so it is charged to us and never credited — direction: inflates our ratio, by an amount a deeper graph would show and this row cannot. Ours additionally gates on the comparator before marking anything downstream, and the derivation here always changes, so that gate never saves us a wake-up.

reading.floor: the object a person keeps instead: a frame number and a queue
reading.caveat: NOT A LIKE-FOR-LIKE FLOOR. Nobody hand-writes a database; the nearest thing is the bookkeeping a person keeps beside their `Map`, which is a frame counter and a list of what to repaint. Ours constructs an unused-slot collector, a channel with its frame record, clock, error policy, pending-effect list, three handler sets and seven bound arrows, and the root that holds both. Direction: inflates our ratio without limit, and it is paid ONCE per application. It is on the table because a price nobody prints is a price nobody believes, not because the multiple means anything. What the absolute figure is MADE OF is what `new-db.vs-the-same-object-graph-by-hand` beside it is for.

reading.floor: the same twenty allocations written out — seven objects, three arrays, three sets and seven closures over them
reading.caveat: THIS ROW EXISTS TO SPLIT `new-db.vs-hand-written-frame-state`, WHOSE FLOOR IS TWO ALLOCATIONS AND WHOSE MULTIPLE THEREFORE HAS NO UPPER BOUND. What that row cannot say is whether the price of a database is its OBJECT GRAPH — twenty allocations that a person keeping the same state would also have made — or something about the class that carries it. This floor allocates the graph and nothing else, read off `OIMDB`, `OIMUnusedSlotCollector`, `OIMChannel` and the default `OIMErrorPolicyLogAndContinue`: the root, the collector and its tracked list, the options object `OIMDB` spreads for the channel, the channel, its frame record with its handler set, the error policy, the pending-effect list, the clock, the subframe-close and after-each-flush sets, the after-each-frame buffer, and the seven bound arrows `enlist`, `collectError`, `runOnceOnSubframeClose`, `openSubframe`, `closeSubframe`, `write` and `writeWithoutFlushCheck`. THE COUNT WAS SEVENTEEN, TRANSCRIBED FROM AN `OIMDB` THAT NO LONGER EXISTS, and no reading of this row taken against that floor is comparable with one taken against this one. WHAT IS LEFT IN THE RATIO is the class: two instance shapes with their field initialisers and the `OIMFlushScheduler` base constructor against object literals built in one place. A reading at 1.00 says the price IS the graph and the only way down is to hold fewer things at birth — which every candidate field would pay for with a test on a path that runs per frame or per write. Above 1.00 it says the construction costs more than what it constructs, and names the size of that. BOTH SIDES DROP EVERYTHING THEY MAKE, so both hand the collector the same shape of garbage at the same rate and the scavenges inside a pass are charged to numerator and denominator alike. Direction: this floor does far MORE than the floor of the row it splits — it is our own graph transcribed — so this ratio is not comparable with any other row in this table. It is a decomposition instrument and not a price.

A population against the container that would have held it. Ours also builds the identity store, the content-change listener list and the content batch list, allocates its index-key positions, reads the defaults off `OIMDB` and `OIMDefaults`, and it keeps the key selector — which is the closure a caller passes and which the floor does not need because the caller writes `row.id` at every call site instead. Direction: inflates our ratio; paid once per population.

reading.ours: createOIMIndexSetDriven over `group` on a population already holding a thousand rows, holdSlotsByKeys every group, then dispose and unholdSlot
reading.floor: build a Map of Sets from the same thousand rows, then clear it
reading.caveat: THE ENGINE WALKS THE POPULATION AGAIN, SO THIS IS A DECLARATION ONCE MORE. It replaces `index-fill.over-a-loaded-population-vs-hand-built-map`, whose caller did the walk and the per-bucket write because the index of that day touched no population; the auto-index files every row it can see into a bucket the moment the bucket is minted (`OIMIndex.collectSourceSlotsForKeys`, through `collectBucketMemberSlotsForKey`), so a `holdSlotsByKeys` over all sixty-four groups is one walk of the thousand rows, one `keyOf` per row, one index-key write per row and one hold per row. No figure recorded under the old id attaches to this one. BOTH SIDES BUILD AND THEN GIVE BACK INSIDE THE CLOCK: ours disposes the index — which drops its listener, releases its index-key position (a second walk of the population, clearing each row's cell) and clears every bucket, unholding each row — and then unholds the sixty-four buckets so each is released; the floor clears every set and then the map. The floor reads `row.group` off held copies; ours reads it through `slot.entity`. What ours buys that the floor cannot: the index keeps filing every later write, and each bucket is an identity that can be subscribed. Direction: inflates our ratio; paid once per index.
